title: PM calls on Australians to reject politics of division
text:
Program:PM

Mon 8 Jun 2026 at 5:00pm

Presented by

The Prime Minister has made an extraordinary appeal to Australians about the nature of the political debate in this country.

Anthony Albanese has joined others in condemning a sexist campaign against Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan.

He says violent and sexist language is too prevalent and he's calling on Australians to reject the politics of division.

Featured:

Anthony Albanese, Prime MinisterJulia Gillard, Former Prime MinisterPauline Hanson, One Nation Leader

This mobile billboard featuring 'Ditch the Witch' has been seen around central Melbourne.(Supplied)

Stephanie Smail: The Prime Minister has made an extraordinary appeal to Australians about the nature of the political debate in this country. Anthony Albanese has joined others in condemning a sexist campaign against Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan. He says violent and sexist language is too prevalent and he's calling on Australians to reject the politics of division. Rachel Mealey reports.

Rachel Mealey: Another week, another opinion poll showing one nation ahead of Labor. The Prime Minister says Australians are sending him a clear message.

Anthony Albanese: To paraphrase, it's the economy stupid. It's always the economy that sets the parameters for debate.

Rachel Mealey: The latest news poll figures continue the recent trend and show one nation's popularity surging, while support for the major parties is falling away. Anthony Albanese says his government acknowledges that economic pressures are driving everyday Australians into the arms of one nation.

Anthony Albanese: Many people feel that the system isn't working for them, that they're working for the economy, not the economy working for them. That they're working hard, struggling to save, can't get their own roof over their head, for example. We want to make sure that we put in place mechanisms that do make a difference. Not political easy decisions, but the right decisions. And that if governments don't respond to that, there'll be a continued rise in populism, be it of the right or the left. It's something that we're seeing. We're seeing globally.

Rachel Mealey: He's called for Australians to be more patriotic and reject the politics of division.

Anthony Albanese: I want an Australia that is united, one that has social cohesion at our core, one that respects people for who they are, but is patriotic about all of us being Australians.

Rachel Mealey: The Prime Minister wants to see the temperature turned down in political debates, fearing what could happen if the mood doesn't change.

Anthony Albanese: What I don't want to do is to have a press conference in this courtyard after a tragedy.

Rachel Mealey: He singled out a sexist attack on Victoria's Premier, Jacinta Allan. Billboards mounted on trucks have been seen in Melbourne for the past few weeks, which depict the Premier wearing a pointed hat, alongside the slogan, Ditch the Witch.

Anthony Albanese: The sexist campaign targeting the Victorian Premier is totally unacceptable and has no place in public life. We want to encourage women to enter public life and it should be a contest of ideas, not personal attacks.

Rachel Mealey: Anthony Albanese pointed to rising rates of personal threats against politicians.

Anthony Albanese: You can have a disagreement with people's policy position by all means. You don't have to denigrate people in such a personal way. It has got to stop. Young girls will see that depiction of a Premier as a witch, just like the denigration that Julia Gillard suffered from as Prime Minister. And it is just not on.

Rachel Mealey: In 2012, Julia Gillard stood in Parliament to deliver this address.

Julia Gillard: I will not be lectured about sexism and misogyny by this man. I will not. And the government will not be lectured about sexism and misogyny by this man. Not now, not ever.

Rachel Mealey: That speech followed then opposition leader Tony Abbott standing with protesters outside Parliament House who carried signs calling her a witch. Today, former Prime Minister Julia Gillard made a rare political statement. In a letter posted on social media, she says, I am disgusted to see the use of the slogan Ditch the Witch in Victoria aimed at Premier Jacinta Allen. This was a slogan used against me as Prime Minister 15 years ago. She goes on to say, whoever funded the billboards bearing these signs should be outed for what they are, unimaginative, ugly sexists. One nation leader, Pauline Hanson, was less sympathetic towards the Victorian Premier.

Pauline Hanson: Suck it up, sweetheart. Right? If you've seen what's happened to me over the years, I remember years ago Tim Fisher called me a witch and I should be burned at the stake. So I've been tagged that long before you. So anyway, it's just toughen up.

Stephanie Smail: One nation leader, Pauline Hanson, ending that report from Rachel Mealey.
